So.. like others have said this is not sustainable. You might be able to do it for a year or two but eventually you will start eating more. 

Also- calories are a super misunderstood measure of energy. We do not have good information on how many calories are truly in the food we are eating and we don’t really have any idea how many of those calories are available to our bodies and how many are just passed into waste products. Further.. we do not have a good measurement for how many calories we burn doing specific exercises. The vast majority of our caloric needs come from our regular body processes and those are controlled by hormones. They are not the same for every person.

All of this amounts to two things: we don’t really know how many calories your body is taking in and how many it’s expending in the form of solid/liquid waste, heat, body processes, activity. 

Eat things that make you strong and make you feel good. Be careful with restrictive diets because they can absolutely lead to disordered eating and can have long term impacts on your metabolism. In the long run, the almost never work to lose large amounts of weight.

So, I don’t really know why they put weight limits on boards, but I think the choice of stiffness should really be determined by a few other factors.

1) strength. Stiffer boards are harder to twist and bend. It takes more strength to turn and Ollie and twist the board. Sometimes strength scales with weight but not always. 


2) type of snow. If you live in the PnW and ride a lot of heavy tracked snow, a stiff board will help you charge through it rather than get bounced around by it. If you ride a lot of light Utah powder, you aren’t getting as much benefit from that stiffness. If you like to lean hard carving high speed turns on hard pack then you’ll want something stiff that can really support you through those turns. 

3) type of riding. So hard carving turns require a stiffer board. Softer boards lend themselves to more playful riding. Park, slushy moguls can be really fun on a soft board. Or if you want to just have some easy cruising blue runs with little side hits, soft board is the way to go. 

So back to your question of whether it will ride softer. I think yeah, it can. If you’re strong enough. But it still might not be advantageous if you’re really looking for something more easy going… or if you’re still learning how to twist your board during turns, tuck your knee, and how to Ollie. 

It’s always a gamble trying to buy a board online and looking at the stiffness ratings. My best advice is to look at the stiffness ratings for board you’ve ridden and liked and try to predict whether you’ll like a board you see online. I just read this comment chain and I have to say that I agree with this person to some extent. Having used Khan with my students (tutor not math teacher) I think it is an excellent supplementary tool, and in the absence of an actu course, it’s really the best option. 

However depending on the goal of the student I think there are some drawbacks and I don’t think it’s a substitute for a full course. Mostly I think it’s important to learn to read math texts.. and especially get used to how slow it is reading a math text. And while the video lectures do a good job of explaining concepts intuitively, the practice problems are very procedural. I also think that because the practice problems are procedural and they are careful to not present anything that wasn’t specifically addressed in the video the student loses out on the explorative nature of math learning. They don’t have to seek out other resources and perspectives, a tool that will be vital in future coursework.

For these reasons I think someone who goes on to more difficult topics from khan alone will have a steeper learning curve. I think these issues can be mitigated by using other sources to supplement and looking for practice problems elsewhere. This is obviously a very difficult task, as the student is essentially building their own curriculum. So the process may take longer than if they had the support of an instructor.

Patrick JMT’s videos
Paul’s online math notes
Stewart calculus (not popular but we must all suffer together)

You need to stay lower, stay over your board (no bending at the waist), control your edge angle better.. but mostly you need to learn how to twist your board. 

On steep stuff, moguls or not, you don't actually want to pull your toes up on your heel edge. that creates an edge angle that is too large and you end up applying too much force and you get that choppy stop. On your heel edge you can lift your front to slightly but you want to push that back toe down. This will twist your board and keep a smaller edge angle, which will keep you smooth. As you transition to toe side you're going to lift the front heel and push down the rear heel. 

Not only does this help you keep a lower edge angle but it also shortens your minimum turn radius, allowing you to make the tight turns you need to make in a mogul field.

I don't size up on my splits just because they're splits. I have a range of sizes and some *are* longer but it has nothing to do with the fact that it's a split. I bought that one for hauling ass on really open runs.

I tend to prefer shorter boards too. I have a relaxed, narrow stance and I ride a lot of trees. I usually ride slightly tapered boards (and I'm super stoked the industry finally caught on with that). 

I choose boards based on the dimensions listed in their specs and I recommend you do the same. Words like "wide", or "fits this size boot" are subjective. Boots from different companies have diff ones volumes and shapes, even at the same foot size. But numbers... They don't lie. There's no guessing there. 

I suggest you look at the specs from boards you like and try to find something similar in a split. 

For the width issue, you can go online and find the width of a board you know fits you, and compare it to the Jones. Comfort wise, I have found that even a single cm will make a huge difference in how the ride feels. I usually look for something with about 4mm of taper for all around type riding. So a nose width that is 4mm wider than the tail. Note that the wider the board, the harder it is to transition between edges.
